1. Uranium fuel cycle:  
- U3O8 (yellowcake): Dominant global company is Cameco (Canada); Western non-Russian option is also Cameco, with significant production in Canada (e.g., Key Lake) and Kazakhstan operations. No meaningful gap; Cameco is the clear Western leader.  
- UF6 (conversion): Dominant global company is Uranium One Group (Russia); dominant Western non-Russian option is Honeywell Uranium Hexafluoride Processing Facility in Metropolis, Illinois, USA, with additional capacity from Orano (France) at La Hague. Orano has sufficient capacity to serve Western needs, though global conversion capacity is concentrated, and Russia historically supplied a large share; as of 2024–2026, Orano and Honeywell are scaling to offset Russian volumes, but no quantified gap is publicly precise.  
- Enriched UF6: Dominant global company is Rosatom (Russia); dominant Western non-Russian option is Urenco (Netherlands/UK/USA), with enrichment plants in Capenhurst (UK), Piketon/Paducah (USA via Centrus), and Eunuclear partnerships. Centrus Energy can produce up to 20% enriched UF6 at Paducah; gap exists for higher enrichment levels (e.g., >20% up to 90%) where Russian supplies dominated, but Urenco and Centrus are expanding to cover LEU and some MLEU needs.  
- UO2 pellet: Dominant global company is Kazatomprom (Kazakhstan); dominant Western non-Russian option is Orano (France) with facilities in Romans-sur-Isère and Pierrelatte, and Westinghouse in the USA. Orano has robust pellet production; no major capacity gap reported.  
- Fuel assembly: Dominant global company is Rosatom; dominant Western non-Russian option is Westinghouse (USA) with facilities in Columbia, South Carolina, and EDF joint ventures; also Framatome (France/USA) and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (Japan). Western capacity is expanding to meet non-Russian demand, but lead times are long; specific gap quantification is not publicly precise.

2. HALEU is High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium, typically defined as uranium-235 enrichment between 20% and 90% (commonly 20% LEU to 90% LEU, with 15–20% being a common operational band for many SMRs). As of 2026, companies that have demonstrated HALEU production at non-pilot scale include Centrus Energy (USA) with its AC100 facility producing ~20% enriched UF6 at scale, and Urenco (through its European facilities) with demonstrated HALEU flows; other vendors such as Orano and international consortia are in advanced testing but not yet at full non-pilot production. Relevant US DOE programs include the HALEU Program under the Office of Nuclear Energy, with funding instruments such as the Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP) cost-sharing awards and the Nuclear Energy Enabling Technologies (NEET) program grants; additionally, the DOE’s HALEU Production Initiative provides procurement and market assurance funding to support domestic production build-out.

3. Westinghouse’s TVS-WR fuel is designed for VVER-1000 reactors and uses an improved pellet and cladding system (e.g., higher enrichment UO2 pellets and advanced Zircaloy cladding) to provide better performance and safety margins compared to legacy designs; it is tailored for non-Russian fuel supply chains. In contrast, Rosatom’s TVSA-T fuel is optimized for Russian VVER designs with specific geometric and material configurations that align with Russian safety and operational standards. Utilities that have switched include certain Eastern European operators (e.g., specific units in Ukraine and Slovakia) that have transitioned to Westinghouse fuel to reduce Russian dependence. Technical issues included dimensional and material compatibility differences requiring revised reactor physics modeling and in-core inspections, while licensing issues involved regulatory approvals in host countries (e.g., Ukrainian regulator approvals and subsequent EU stress tests) that delayed full fleet conversion; these have been navigated through phased reloads and engineering evaluations.

4. Heavy-duty gas turbine market (H-class and J-class):  
- GE Vernova: H-class (7HA.01/7HA.02) and J-class (6B/7B) backlogs are substantial but specific public backlog numbers are not routinely disclosed; recent announcements indicate strong order books through 2027–2030.  
- Siemens Energy: H-class (SGT5-8000H) and J-class (SGT6-5000F) have significant backlogs, with public statements noting multi-year order queues; exact backlog capacity figures are not published in detail.  
- Mitsubishi Power: H-class (M501J) and J-class (M501G) similarly have robust order visibility through 2028–2030, with public disclosures indicating sustained demand.  
Realistic slot lead-time for an order placed in 2026 is approximately 36–48 months for new units, with site preparation and grid connection adding further time. Utilities and hyperscalers that have locked forward slots include Microsoft and Google (for data center power) with agreements extending to 2028–2030, and specific utility PPAs (e.g., in the USA and Europe) securing deliveries through this window; precise names are often confidential, but public procurement notices reference long-term turbine supply agreements.

5. LNG:  
Top 5 liquefaction operators (by capacity) are typically: QatarEnergy (Ras Laffan, North Field), Saudi Arabian Oil Company (Saudi Aramco, Ras Tanura), Equinor (Norway), Shell (Qatar), and BP (Trinidad and Tobago) or TotalEnergies (Qatar); listing the largest five single plants is complex due to expansions, but Ras Laffan (Qatar), Dahej (India), Gorgon (Australia), SEGAS (Egypt), and Exports Terminal (Qatar) are among the largest.  
Top 3 LNG carrier shipyards: Samsung Heavy Industries (Geoje, South Korea), Hyundai Heavy Industries (Ulsan, South Korea), and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (Nagasaki, Japan). GTT membrane technology matters because it enables higher cargo capacity and lower boil-off rates through advanced insulation systems (e.g., NO96, Mark III), making new-build vessels more economically viable for long-haul routes; this technology influences chartering economics and newbuilding order decisions. Disruption to membrane licensing or shipyard slots in 2024–2026 includes increased demand stretching delivery slots (often 3–5 year waits), and licensing complexities for new membrane designs across classification societies, but no major supply shocks have been reported; however, some shipyards are prioritizing LNG carriers over other vessels, extending lead times.

6. SMR designs with OECD regulatory milestones by 2026:  
- NuScale Power VOYGR-6 (US NRC design certification achieved, lead vendor NuScale, pilot site: Idaho National Laboratory/DOE project, also Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems).  
- GE-Hitachi BWRX-300 (US NRC design certification in process, lead vendor GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy, pilot site: Ontario Power Generation in Canada; US NRC SDA approval steps noted).  
- Rolls-Royce SMR (UK GDA milestone reached, lead vendor Rolls-Royce SMR, pilot site: potential Wylfa Newydd in Wales, with UK regulatory approvals advancing).
